P0100.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit
P0100.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or supply wire open
Sensor faulty internally (broken element, failed electronics)
Supply fuse or relay failed
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)

P0101.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0101.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed.

causes.label: Air leak between sensor and engine (cracked or loose intake duct, boost leak)
Contaminated sensing element (oil from oiled sport filter, dust)
Leaking or disconnected crankcase ventilation
Clogged or wrongly fitted air filter, modified intake
Aged sensor or poor contact in the wiring

symptoms: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems
Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response
Higher consumption, often with lean codes P0171/P0174

P0102.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Low
P0102.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0102 means the signal is below its electrical lower limit – a frequency that is too low or a voltage that is too low. Documented limits: GM petrol 450 Hz or less, GM diesel below 276 Hz, Ford digital below 1.5 kHz for 5 s, Ford analogue below 0.244 V. 'Low' describes the signal: typically an open or grounded signal wire, missing supply voltage or failed electronics. Saab notes that a large leak between sensor and throttle can also cause it. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine runs on a calculated substitute value.

causes.label: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector corroded or loose
Sensor electronics failed
Missing supply voltage (fuse, relay) or poor ground
Large leak or disconnected duct between sensor and throttle

symptoms: Lack of power, hesitation, substitute value mode

P0103.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit High
P0103.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0103 means the signal is above its electrical upper limit. Documented limits: GM petrol 14,500 Hz or more, GM diesel above 12,500 Hz, Saab 9-4X above about 15,150 Hz, Ford analogue above 4.785 V (checked only below 4,000 rpm so that high load is not mistaken for a fault). Typical causes are a signal wire shorted to a voltage source, failed sensor electronics or interference from a harness routed too close to ignition coils, relays or motors. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine switches to a calculated air mass.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to voltage or to the supply wire
Sensor electronics failed
Interference from harness routed near ignition coils, relays or motors
Water in the connector or on the element

symptoms: Substitute value mode, lack of power

P0104.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0104.description: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0104 covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal without a permanent low or high fault – the classic sign of a loose contact. In Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary the code is set once more than 25 short open or short-circuit events have been counted. GM and Saab do not list P0104 in the documents checked; there such dropouts end up under P0102/P0103 or P0101. The trip count is not stated by Ford. Diagnosis means moving the harness while watching the live signal and checking terminals for corrosion and weak tension.

causes.label: Loose contact at the sensor connector (corrosion, spread terminals, broken latch)
Chafed or partly broken wire moved by the engine
Sensor electronics dropping out (temperature-dependent)
Poor ground or electrical interference

symptoms: Check engine light on, may go out again
Occasional hesitation, misfire-like stumble, flat spot

P0105.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit
P0105.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0105 is the general circuit fault and is rarely used today: most petrol engines report low, high and intermittent separately (P0107–P0109). It appears mainly where the fault cannot be broken down further – Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the digital SENT sensor reports a bad status or an out-of-limit value for 5 s (lost communication is a separate U code), and Bosch EDC16 diesels use it with a fault type byte, for example signal below 0.2 V. Saab then substitutes 101.3 kPa, limits torque and switches off EGR and boost control.

causes.label: Connector or wiring to the sensor open, shorted or loose
MAP sensor faulty (oiled, failed internally, SENT status fault)
Sensor hose disconnected, vacuum or boost leak
5 V reference pulled down by another sensor on the same circuit
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel)
Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol)

P0106.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0106.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0106 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or drifting. Two tests are common. With the engine stopped, all pressures equalise, so MAP must match ambient (and boost) pressure; Ford allows 1.5–3 inHg. While running, MAP is compared with a value modelled from air mass, throttle and speed – GM blames the MAP sensor above about 23–30 kPa error, with two trips on petrol and one on diesel. Turbo engines with three sensors find the odd one out by majority. Besides the sensor, intake or boost leaks often cause it.

causes.label: Vacuum leak at the intake manifold or boost leak (hose, clamp, charge air cooler)
Sensor oiled or sooted, port blocked (EGR soot), characteristic drifted
High resistance in signal, reference or ground wire
Comparison sensor wrong, or mechanical cause (dirty throttle, EGR stuck open)

symptoms: Higher consumption, black smoke possible on diesels
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines

P0107.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Low
P0107.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0107 means the signal voltage is below its lower limit. 'Low' refers to the voltage, not to a real low pressure: typically the signal wire is grounded, the signal or 5 V reference is open, or the sensor has failed. A short on another sensor sharing the same reference can pull it down too, so GM often sees several codes at once. Documented limits: GM below 3.3 % of 5 V (about 0.17 V), GM/Saab 2.0T below 0.19 V for 4 s, Ford petrol below 0.19 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.1 V. GM petrol needs two trips, GM diesel one. A modelled value replaces the reading.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing)
5 V reference shorted by another faulty sensor on the same circuit
MAP sensor failed internally
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Hard starting, rough idle, stalling possible
Wrong mixture from substitute value, higher consumption
Loss of power or limp mode on turbo and diesel engines

P0108.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit High
P0108.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0108 means the signal voltage is above its upper limit – typically an open ground (low reference), a signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage, or a failed sensor. Like P0107 it describes the voltage, not real overpressure; genuinely excessive boost is P0234. Documented limits: GM petrol above 86 % of 5 V, GM diesel above 97 %, GM/Saab 2.0T above 4.80 V for 4 s, Ford above 4.88–4.96 V for 5 s. The engine substitutes a modelled value, which often makes the mixture too rich; turbo engines limit boost.

causes.label: Ground (low reference) wire open or connector corroded
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
MAP sensor failed internally
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Rough idle, loss of power or limp mode on turbo engines

P0109.title: Manifold Absolute Pressure/Barometric Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent
P0109.description: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0109 counts brief range violations of the signal that are too short for P0107/P0108 – the typical signature of a loose contact. Ford counts excursions below 0.024 V or above 4.96 V and sets the code after 25 events per drive cycle (2020–2023; ten in 2012). Ford treated it as a code without warning light in 2012 but lights the MIL in 2020–2023, so the warning-light behaviour depends on the manufacturer. GM does not use P0109 in the tables checked; there short dropouts accumulate in P0107/P0108.

causes.label: Loose contact at the MAP connector, terminals spread or corroded
Chafed or broken wire that makes contact with engine movement
Sensor with internal dropouts
Ground problem or control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)

P010A.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit
P010A.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010A is the general circuit fault of sensor B: no usable signal at all, just like P0100 for sensor A. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary lists it for a broken element of digital sensor B, with the same limit as sensor A (period above 1.3 ms for half a second); which engines carry sensor B is not stated. GM's twin-turbo V6 only uses the other sensor B codes. The engine can run on values calculated from manifold pressure, throttle and the remaining sensor.

causes.label: Connector or wiring of sensor B open
Sensor B faulty internally (broken element)
Supply of sensor B missing (fuse, relay)
Control module input faulty

P010B.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P010B.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010B is the plausibility fault of sensor B: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. GM checks it like sensor A against a model built from the other sensors (manifold pressure, boost, throttle, sensor A) and fails it above 20 g/s deviation, with two trips. For the VR30DDTT Nissan names a loose or leaking left-hand intake pipe as the main cause and warns against touching or dismantling the sensor. Other causes match P0101: a soiled element, a clogged filter on that side or a boost leak.

causes.label: Intake pipe on the sensor B side leaking or not seated
Sensor B element contaminated (oil, dust)
Air filter on that side clogged or wrongly fitted
Boost leak on that bank, or sensor/connector problem

P010C.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Low
P010C.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010C means the signal of sensor B is below its electrical lower limit – the counterpart of P0102. GM's twin-turbo V6 sets it at 400 Hz or less (300 failed out of 375 samples, two trips); Ford's digital sensor B below 1.5 kHz for 5 s. The usual causes are an open or grounded signal wire, a corroded connector, missing supply or failed sensor electronics. The engine continues with a calculated substitute value.

causes.label: Signal wire of sensor B open or grounded, connector corroded
Sensor B electronics failed
Supply or ground of sensor B faulty
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Lack of power, substitute value mode

P010D.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit High
P010D.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010D means the signal of sensor B is above its electrical upper limit – the counterpart of P0103. GM's twin-turbo V6 sets it at 14,500 Hz or more (two trips); Ford's digital sensor B when the signal period drops below 83 microseconds, i.e. above roughly 12 kHz, for 5 s. Typical causes are a signal wire shorted to voltage, failed sensor electronics or interference from nearby ignition or actuator wiring. A substitute value is used.

causes.label: Signal wire of sensor B shorted to voltage
Sensor B electronics failed
Interference from harness routing
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Substitute value mode, lack of power
Rich mixture and higher consumption possible

P010E.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P010E.description: Sensor B is a second mass air flow sensor in a second intake path, found on engines with two air filter boxes – for example the Nissan VR30DDTT twin-turbo V6 (where sensor B belongs to bank 2) or GM's 3.0 litre twin-turbo V6. P010E covers brief dropouts or jumps in the signal of sensor B without a lasting low or high fault, the counterpart of P0104. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary sets it after more than 25 short open or short-circuit events; GM's twin-turbo V6 does not use it, and Ford does not state the trip count. The usual cause is a loose contact at the connector or a chafed wire that opens as the engine moves.

causes.label: Loose contact at the sensor B connector
Chafed or partly broken wire
Sensor B electronics dropping out
Poor ground or interference

symptoms: Check engine light on, may come and go

P010F.title: Mass or Volume Air Flow Sensor A/B Correlation
P010F.description: Engines with two intake paths have two mass air flow sensors, A and B. On a symmetrical V engine both sides should draw about the same amount of air, so the readings can be compared with each other. P010F is set when both signals are electrically valid but differ by more than allowed; the code does not say which side is wrong. No manufacturer document using exactly this code or its threshold was found: GM's twin-turbo V6 and Nissan's VR30DDTT assess each sensor separately against a model (P0101/P010B). The description therefore rests on the CARB requirement for plausibility checks and on component sources for engines with two sensors. Typical causes are a leaking intake pipe or a soiled sensor on one side.

causes.label: Air leak or loose intake pipe on one side
One of the two sensors contaminated or aged
Air filter on one side clogged or wrongly fitted
Turbocharger or boost problem on one bank
Contact resistance in connector or wiring

symptoms: Mixture codes for one bank (P0171/P0174) possible

P0110.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Bank 1
P0110.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0110 is the general circuit fault. With a conventional analogue sensor most manufacturers report low and high signals separately (P0112/P0113), so P0110 mainly appears in two cases: with digital (SENT) sensors that combine air mass and temperature, where it stands for lost communication or an implausible status (Ford diesel 2023, after about 5 s), and in some Bosch systems as a collective code whose fault type byte tells open circuit from short to ground. The control module then uses a substitute temperature; some systems also limit torque.

causes.label: Connector or wiring to the sensor open or corroded
Sensor or mass air flow sensor with built-in temperature sensor faulty
Sensor supply or ground disturbed
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Reduced power or torque limitation on some systems
Otherwise usually inconspicuous; cold start may be slightly worse

P0111.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance Bank 1
P0111.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0111 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. The usual test runs at key-on after a long soak (Ford 6 h, GM 8 h): the intake air sensor is compared with other temperature sensors such as coolant, cylinder head, charge air cooler or IAT2, which should all read about the same. GM flags it above about 25 °C deviation, Ford above about 17 °C; Ford first confirms with a drive above 40 mph because sunshine can warm a sensor, and also sets P0111 if the air reads over 66 °C while driving. A detected block heater suspends the test. Two consecutive trips are needed.

causes.label: Sensor drifting or stuck at one value (ageing, oil from crankcase ventilation)
Contact resistance at connector or wiring distorts the reading
Comparison sensor (coolant, IAT2, charge air cooler) wrong
Undetected preheater, heat soak or sensor mounted near a heat source

symptoms: Slightly changed idle, power or cold start possible
Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P0112.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low Bank 1
P0112.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0112 means the signal is below its valid range. With an NTC sensor that points to a short to ground in the signal wire or an internally shorted sensor, and the control module would read an implausibly hot value (GM about 150 °C). Documented limits: Ford petrol below 0.244 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.10 V, GM below 62 ohms. The circuit is monitored continuously; GM needs two trips. Some systems then use the coolant temperature, capped at 40 °C, as a substitute and limit torque.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed insulation)
Sensor shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Retarded ignition, reduced power or torque limit on some systems

P0113.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High Bank 1
P0113.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0113 means the signal is above its valid range. With an NTC sensor that is typically an open circuit – connector off, broken wire, open sensor or missing ground – or a short to a voltage source, and the module would read an extremely cold value (GM about −60 °C). Documented limits: Ford petrol above 4.96 V for 5 s, Ford diesel above 4.91 V, GM above about 127 kilohms. A classic cause is a sensor left unplugged after an air filter change; one manufacturer bulletin describes broken wires at the connector caused by harness tension. Monitoring is continuous, GM needs two trips.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or loose, or wire broken
Sensor open internally
Sensor return (ground) wire open
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Slightly richer mixture and higher consumption possible

P0114.title: Intake Air Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic Bank 1
P0114.description: Intake air temperature sensor 1 is the first air temperature sensor in the intake path; depending on the vehicle it is built into the mass air flow sensor, mounted near the air filter or, on some naturally aspirated GM engines, fitted in the intake manifold. Most versions are NTC thermistors in a 5 V divider: the hotter the air, the lower the signal voltage. P0114 covers an unsteady signal. Air temperature changes slowly, so rapid jumps point to the wiring rather than the air. Ford counts short excursions out of range that are each too brief for P0112/P0113 and sets the code after ten of them in one drive cycle. GM evaluates noise within the valid range: if the readings taken every 100 ms add up to more than 80 °C of movement within one second, in four of five seconds, the sample counts as failed. GM needs two trips. Typical culprit is a loose contact that opens with engine movement.

causes.label: Loose contact at the connector (corrosion, weak terminal tension)
Partly broken wire that opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal contact problem
Electrical interference or ground fault

symptoms: Occasional brief stumble or rough idle possible

P0115.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit
P0115.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0115 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. Today it has largely been replaced by P0117, P0118 and P0119; GM and Ford do not set it in the tables checked. Older or individual systems still use it as a collective code, for example Saab Trionic T5 (1998). The circuit is monitored continuously; when it fails, the module uses a substitute value and many systems run the radiator fan permanently.

causes.label: Connector corroded or loose, terminal spread
Broken or chafed signal or ground wire
Sensor faulty internally (short, open, coolant inside)
Control module input or 5 V supply faulty

P0116.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Range/Performance
P0116.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0116 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but not believable. Most often it checks for a sensor stuck too warm. After a long soak (GM 8 h, Ford 6 h) coolant must be close to intake air temperature; GM fails it above about 19 °C difference without a detected block heater, Ford if it reads over 110 °C or sits at 79–110 °C. Ford diesels instead check whether coolant warms fast enough in frost. A sensor stuck warm suppresses cold-start enrichment and can defeat the thermostat monitor, which is why CARB requires this test. GM uses one or two trips depending on the engine.

causes.label: Sensor drifting and reading too warm (ageing, coolant ingress)
Corrosion or contact resistance in connector or wiring
Block heater or preheater not detected
Comparison sensor (intake air, ambient) wrong
Control module calibration

P0117.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Low
P0117.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0117 means the signal voltage is too low, so the sensor would report an implausibly hot engine (around 140–160 °C). Usual causes are a signal wire shorted to ground, coolant or moisture in the connector, or an internally shorted sensor. Limits: GM below 55 ohms, Ford petrol below 0.244 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.10 V, Mitsubishi below 0.1 V for 2 s. Mitsubishi then calculates with 80 °C; GM/Saab switch the radiator fan on and the A/C compressor off. GM needs two trips. On Ford engines with a head temperature sensor the equivalent is P1290.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing, pinched harness)
Sensor shorted internally or coolant inside the sensor
Moisture or coolant in the connector
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Hard cold start (no enrichment, engine reported hot)

P0118.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit High
P0118.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0118 means the signal voltage sits near the 5 V reference, so the sensor would report about −40 °C. Typical causes are an unplugged or corroded connector, a broken signal or sensor ground wire, an open sensor or a short to voltage. Limits: GM above 134 kilohms (only after 10 s running, so genuine cold is not misread), Ford petrol above 4.96 V for 5 s, Ford diesel above 4.91 V, GM/Saab below −39 °C for 4 s. Without a substitute strategy the mixture would be far too rich; GM/Saab run the fan and switch off the A/C. On Ford engines with a head temperature sensor the equivalent is P1289.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, contact open
Broken signal or sensor ground wire
Sensor open internally
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Rich mixture, higher consumption, possibly black smoke or fuel smell

P0119.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0119.description: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. Coolant temperature can only change slowly because of the thermal mass involved. P0119 is set when the reading jumps faster than physically possible. GM calculates, every second, a window for the next valid value from the previous reading and a sensor time constant of 13 s; readings outside it in three of four samples count as a fault, monitored continuously over two trips. GM/Saab set it after more than 4 s of abrupt changes and then run the radiator fan. Typical causes are loose contacts or a harness chafing as the engine moves.

causes.label: Loose contact or corroded connector pins
Harness chafing that briefly grounds or opens with engine movement
Sensor with internal crack or contact fault
Air pockets at the sensor (poorly bled cooling system)

symptoms: Radiator fan switches on for no reason
Occasional rough running or idle fluctuation

P011A.title: Engine Coolant Temperature Sensor 1/2 Correlation
P011A.description: Some engines have two coolant temperature sensors that check each other. P011A is set when both are electrically fine but their readings differ more than a calibrated amount under conditions where they should agree. Mazda documents the code for the 2013–2016 CX-5 and 2014–2016 Mazda6: sensor 2 sits in the heater hose, and a clogged heater core keeps it noticeably colder, so P011A often comes with weak cabin heat although both sensors are good. Mazda's check is to compare both sensors with ambient temperature after an overnight soak and then the temperature difference across the heater hoses. A block heater used below 0 °C can also trigger it.

causes.label: Clogged heater core or restricted coolant flow at sensor 2
One of the two sensors drifting
Air in the cooling system or low coolant level
Block heater use in frost
Contact resistance at one sensor

P011B.title: Engine Coolant Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation
P011B.description: After a long standstill the coolant and the intake air should both have settled close to ambient temperature. P011B compares the two sensors at start-up and is set when they disagree without either sensor showing a circuit fault. In the documented GM/Saab version the engine must have been off for more than 10 hours with no preheater detected; the fault counts if coolant reads at least 20 °C above intake air, or intake air at least 30 °C above coolant, and the coolant reading barely moves (2 °C or less) in the first 45 s. The code does not say which sensor is wrong – that has to be found by comparing both with the actual ambient temperature. Toyota resolved false settings on some 2015 V6 engines with new software. Ford and GM report the same idea under the individual sensor codes.

causes.label: Coolant temperature sensor stuck or drifting
Intake air temperature sensor drifting or heat-soaked
Undetected preheater or uneven cooling
Contact resistance at a sensor connector or ground
Control module software (false setting, update available)

symptoms: With a wrong coolant reading: poor cold start, higher consumption or odd fan behaviour
Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P011C.title: Charge Air Cooler Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation Bank 1
P011C.description: On turbocharged engines a charge air cooler temperature sensor sits downstream of the compressor, usually after the charge air cooler, and intake air temperature sensor 1 sits upstream near the air filter. While driving they differ by design, because compression heats the air. After a long standstill, however, both should read nearly the same, so the check runs at start-up. P011C is set when the two bank 1 sensors disagree there, without naming the faulty one. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Ford performs the same comparison after 6 hours (tolerance about 17 °C on petrol, 16 °C on the 2023 diesel) but reports the outlier as P007B, P0111 or P00CE.

causes.label: Charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck
Intake air temperature sensor 1 drifting
Contact resistance at connector or shared ground
Undetected preheating or uneven cooling (sun, residual heat)

symptoms: Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P011D.title: Charge Air Cooler Temperature/Intake Air Temperature Correlation Bank 2
P011D.description: This is the bank 2 counterpart of P011C and only exists on engines with two separate intake paths, each with its own charge air cooler temperature sensor and intake air temperature sensor – for example V engines with twin turbochargers and separate charge air coolers. After a long standstill both bank 2 sensors should read nearly the same; if they disagree at start-up, without either showing a circuit fault, P011D is set. The code does not identify which sensor is wrong. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the check follows the same principle Ford uses for bank 1 after 6 hours, with a preheater suspending it.

causes.label: Bank 2 charge air cooler temperature sensor drifting, oily or stuck
Bank 2 intake air temperature sensor drifting
Contact resistance at connector or ground
Undetected preheating or uneven cooling

symptoms: Code often returns only after an overnight soak

P011E.title: Engine Coolant Temperature 1 / Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
P011E.description: After a long standstill, typically six to eight hours, the coolant should have cooled to roughly the outside air temperature measured by the ambient sensor in the bumper or mirror. P011E compares coolant temperature sensor 1 with the ambient sensor at start-up and is set when they differ beyond a calibrated limit and no preheater was detected. The code does not say which of the two sensors is wrong. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on the CARB requirement for coolant sensor plausibility and on the same cold-soak comparison that Ford (reported as P0071), GM/Saab and Mazda perform under other codes.

causes.label: Coolant temperature sensor 1 drifting
Ambient temperature sensor drifting or affected by engine heat or sun
Preheater not detected
Contact resistance in one sensor's connector or wiring

P011F.title: Engine Coolant Temperature 2 / Ambient Air Temperature Correlation
P011F.description: This is the counterpart of P011E for the second coolant temperature sensor and only exists on engines that have one – for example at the engine outlet, the radiator or in the heater circuit. After a long standstill sensor 2 should also read roughly the outside temperature; if it disagrees with the ambient sensor beyond a calibrated limit at start-up, P011F is set without saying which sensor is wrong. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB plus the cold-soak comparisons documented by Mazda (sensor 2 in the heater hose) and Ford under other codes.

causes.label: Coolant temperature sensor 2 drifting
Ambient temperature sensor faulty or influenced
Preheater or block heater
Contact resistance at sensor 2

P0120.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit
P0120.description: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0120 is the general circuit fault, used when the fault cannot be classed as low or high or when the sensor is digital. Ford sets it on digital SENT throttle sensors when the sensor reports an error for more than 4 s, together with the MIL and wrench lamp; Saab Trionic used it as a collective code. GM and Ford's analogue throttles report P0122/P0123 instead. Electronic throttles then fall back to a spring-loaded limp position with limited power.

causes.label: Connector at the throttle body corroded or loose, broken wire
Sensor or throttle body with integrated sensor faulty
5 V reference disturbed (short on another sensor of the same circuit)
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles

P0121.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Range/Performance
P0121.description: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0121 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit the engine's state. Manufacturers check this very differently. GM compares throttle position against air mass and pressures modelled from the other intake sensors and needs two trips; Saab/GM 2011 cut power. Ford used P0121 only on its older second-generation electronic throttle, for more than 7° disagreement between the two sensors, without MIL – newer Fords report that as P2135. Cable throttles (Saab 1997) check that idle voltage stays between 0.24 and 1 V. Carbon on the throttle and worn sensor tracks are typical causes.

causes.label: Carboned or mechanically sticking throttle plate
Worn potentiometer track (signal sticks or jumps)
Air leak or faulty MAF/MAP sensor (model comparison)
Contact resistance in signal or ground wire
Sensor or idle stop misadjusted (cable systems)

symptoms: Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Shift problems on automatics (wrong load signal)

P0122.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Low
P0122.description: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0122 means the signal voltage of sensor A is below its lower limit – electrically meant, not 'throttle closed': typically an open or grounded signal wire or a missing 5 V reference. Limits: Ford below 0.25 V (detected within 1 s), Saab/GM 2011 below 0.3 V for 1 s, Saab cable system below 0.2 V for 5 s. GM treats it as a one-trip fault and switches to reduced engine power; Ford lights the MIL and wrench lamp and continues on the remaining sensor or in limp mode.

causes.label: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Connector at the throttle body loose or corroded
5 V reference missing (open, or shorted by another sensor)
Sensor or throttle body faulty
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Engine barely responds to the pedal or stalls at idle
High idle, A/C switched off (cable systems)

P0123.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit High
P0123.description: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0123 means the signal voltage of sensor A is above its upper limit – usually an open sensor ground, which lets the signal float up to the reference, or a signal wire shorted to 5 V or 12 V. Limits: Ford above 4.75 V (within 1 s), Saab/GM 2011 above 4.8 V for 1 s, Saab cable system above 4.96 V for 5 s. Because GM's sensor 1 runs inverted, a high signal there electrically resembles idle, not full throttle. GM sets it after one trip; electronic throttles go into limp mode.

causes.label: Sensor ground (low reference) open or high-resistance
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or 12 V
Sensor or throttle body faulty
Moisture or corrosion in the connector

symptoms: Check engine light, on electronic throttles also wrench lamp
Limp mode with reduced power ('Reduced Engine Power') on electronic throttles
Raised idle or delayed throttle response

P0124.title: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor/Switch A Circuit Intermittent
P0124.description: Sensor A is, in practice, throttle position sensor 1 at the throttle body; the accelerator pedal has its own codes (P2120 onwards). With a cable-operated throttle there is a single potentiometer (about 0.5 V closed to 4.5 V wide open). Electronic throttles have two sensors sharing a 5 V reference and ground, usually running in opposite directions – on GM throttle sensor 1 falls from 3–4 V at idle to below 1 V at full throttle. P0124 covers short, recurring dropouts of sensor A. The only manufacturer source naming it is Ford's 2020–2023 summary for digital SENT throttle sensors: an error lasting more than 0.4 s sets P0124, one lasting more than 4 s sets P0120, so brief dropouts are kept apart from lasting faults; MIL and wrench lamp come on. GM does not use P0124 in the tables checked – its low/high monitors already catch intermittent shorts. For analogue sensors the description rests on CARB and component information. Typical causes are loose contacts, a chafed harness or a worn potentiometer track.

causes.label: Loose contact in the connector (spread terminals, corrosion)
Chafed or partly broken wire in the harness
Worn potentiometer track (dropout at a certain position)
Sensor electronics faulty (SENT)

symptoms: Check engine light, possibly only intermittently
Limp mode that disappears after restart

P0125.title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Closed Loop Fuel Control
P0125.description: Closed-loop mixture control using the oxygen sensors is only released once the coolant has reached a minimum temperature. CARB requires that this happens within set times – from 2006 two minutes if the engine starts up to 8 °C below the release temperature, five minutes if 8–19 °C below. P0125 means it took too long. Ford checks once per cold start and fails if coolant is still below 10 °C while its model already expects over 27 °C; Mitsubishi expects about 7 °C within 90–300 s and also fails if coolant drops back below 40 °C. Long idling suspends the test. Usual causes are a thermostat stuck open or a sensor reading too cold. GM does not use this code in the tables checked.

causes.label: Thermostat stuck open (especially in cold weather)
Coolant sensor reading too cold or slow (drift, contact resistance)
Low coolant level or air at the sensor
Much idling or coasting in frost
Engine control module

symptoms: Engine warms up slowly, heater stays cold for a long time

P0126.title: Insufficient Coolant Temperature for Stable Operation
P0126.description: The generic title refers to a coolant temperature that is not reached for stable operation, i.e. for releasing further functions and diagnostics; how manufacturers implement it differs. The only implementation documented in a manufacturer source is Subaru's (via the Saab 9-2X service information): there P0126 is a stuck-sensor check – if the coolant signal changes by less than 5 mV during 20 s of driving or idling after start, the sensor counts as frozen. It runs once per drive cycle, lights the MIL after two consecutive cycles and has no fail-safe mode. Other interpretations, closer to a thermostat check, could not be verified in a manufacturer document.

causes.label: Coolant sensor frozen or faulty (resistance does not change)
Thermostat stuck open or low coolant
Contact resistance in connector or wiring
Engine control module

symptoms: Engine and heater warm up slowly

P0127.title: Intake Air Temperature Too High
P0127.description: P0127 is not a circuit fault but a functional check of the air path: the measured intake air temperature is too high for the operating state. The logic is documented for a Bosch EDC16 diesel (Saab 9-3): if the intake air exceeds 130 °C and does not fall below it within 45 s after the exhaust gas recirculation valve is closed, hot exhaust gas is evidently still entering or the sensor is wrong. The engine then disables EGR and runs in limp mode with reduced torque. GM has the code in its diesel software but disabled for US OBD II; Ford reports an overly hot intake air reading as P0111 instead. On other engines a hot reading can also come from warm under-bonnet air being drawn in.

causes.label: EGR valve stuck open or not sealing (diesel)
EGR cooler clogged or bypass flap stuck in bypass
Charge air cooler dirty or airflow through it blocked
Sensor reading wrong, or hot engine-bay air drawn in (loose intake duct)

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit
Knock tendency and retarded ignition on petrol engines

P0128.title: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)
P0128.description: After a cold start the thermostat stays closed so the engine warms up quickly. CARB requires the coolant to reach a temperature at most 11 °C below the thermostat's rated value within a set time. GM models the heat put in (fuel energy minus losses to ambient, cabin heater and coasting) and fails if enough energy has gone in without coolant reaching about 65 °C (55 °C in cold weather). Ford compares the measured value with a modelled one, typically failing below 78 °C with an 89 °C thermostat. The test runs once per drive cycle, pauses with much idling or below about −7 °C, and needs two trips. Usually the thermostat is stuck open; a sensor reading too low is the other suspect.

causes.label: Thermostat stuck open or opening too early
Coolant sensor reading too low, or corrosion and resistance in its circuit
Low coolant level or air in the system
Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck, wrong control)
Driving pattern or conditions (much idling, extreme cold, strong heating)

symptoms: Temperature gauge stays low or drops while driving
Heater does not get properly warm

P0129.title: Barometric Pressure Too Low
P0129.description: The engine control module needs the ambient air pressure for mixture, altitude correction and boost limits. It comes either from a dedicated barometric sensor or from the MAP sensor, read at key-on with the engine stopped and updated at wide-open throttle. P0129 means this value is lower than physically possible – even on the highest drivable passes air pressure stays around 50 kPa, and GM and Ford use 50 kPa as their lower plausibility limit. Usual causes are a MAP or baro sensor reading too low, a blocked sensor port or high resistance in the wiring. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found: GM and Ford file the same finding under P2227.

causes.label: MAP or baro sensor reading too low (dirty, oiled, drifted)
High resistance or corrosion in signal wire or connector
Sensor port or hose blocked
Control module (baro sensor often built in) or software

symptoms: Rich mixture, higher consumption, rough idle

P012A.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P012A.description: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012A is the general circuit fault. Ford's 2023 diesels use a digital SENT sensor here and set P012A when its error flag is raised or the value exceeds a limit for 5 s; lost communication is reported separately (U068B). FCA's 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo could set P012A, P012C and P012D falsely and was fixed with new engine software, so the software level is worth checking before replacing parts. GM's supercharged V8 uses only P012B–P012D. A substitute value, usually ambient pressure, is used.

causes.label: Connector or wiring open, corroded or shorted
Sensor faulty (SENT sensor reports internal error)
Control module software (false setting)
Engine control module faulty

P012B.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P012B.description: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012B is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but stuck or offset. On GM's supercharged 6.2 V8 the sensor must read 50–115 kPa and agree within 10 kPa with MAP and ambient pressure after the engine has been off for more than 8 s; while running, it is compared with modelled values (fault above about 25–30 kPa). GM normally needs two trips, one in some 2019 applications. In operation inlet pressure is slightly below ambient because of filter losses, so a clogged filter or blocked intake lowers it further.

causes.label: Sensor oiled (crankcase vent often joins before the compressor) or drifted
Air filter heavily clogged or intake blocked or collapsed
Leak in the intake pipe between filter and compressor or at the sensor flange
High resistance in the wiring
Comparison sensor (MAP, baro, MAF) wrong or software

symptoms: Loss of power or boost limitation

P012C.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P012C.description: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012C means the signal voltage is below its lower limit – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, an open signal or 5 V reference wire, or a failed sensor. GM's supercharged V8 sets it below 3 % of the 5 V reference (about 0.15 V), with 320 of 400 samples failing, continuously monitored; two trips are normal, one in some 2019 applications. FCA documented false settings on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo that were cured by a software update. A substitute value is used and power may be limited.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or corroded, signal or reference wire open
Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor failed internally
Control module software (false setting)
5 V reference shorted by another sensor

P012D.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P012D.description: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors. P012D means the signal voltage is above its upper limit – typically the signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or an open sensor ground that lets the signal rise to the reference. GM's supercharged LT4/LT5 sets it above 97 % of the reference (about 124 kPa) with 320 of 400 samples failing, monitored continuously; two trips on the LT4, one on the 2019 LT5. FCA documented false settings on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo, fixed by new engine software. The control module substitutes a modelled or ambient value and may limit boost.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor ground open or connector corroded
Sensor faulty internally
Control module software (false setting)

symptoms: Reduced power or limp mode possible

P012E.title: Turbocharger/Supercharger Inlet Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P012E.description: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors. P012E covers a signal that jumps or drops out briefly without staying below or above the circuit limits – typically a loose contact. Such intermittent monitors usually count short limit violations or changes faster than real pressure can move. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found: GM handles jumps of this sensor through its range check P012B and the counting windows of P012C/P012D, and Ford's 2023 diesels report their digital sensor under P012A. The description therefore rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information. A substitute value is used while the fault is present.

causes.label: Loose contact or corrosion at the sensor connector
Broken or chafed wire making intermittent contact
Sensor faulty internally (erratic output)
Control module or software

symptoms: Occasional power reduction or boost fluctuation

P012F.title: Engine Coolant Temperature / Engine Oil Temperature Correlation
P012F.description: P012F compares the coolant temperature sensor with the engine oil temperature sensor. The documented user is Ford's Power Stroke diesel. After a calibration update for the 6.0 litre engine, Ford uses it to monitor oil cooler efficiency: if the oil gets much hotter than the coolant at certain speed and load, the oil-to-coolant heat exchanger is probably clogged, and P012F sets together with the wrench lamp. On the 6.7 litre (2015–2018) several bulletins treat P012F as a false setting – partly below 5 °C ambient – cured by reprogramming the engine module. Ford's 2023 diesels run the cold-start comparison of coolant against oil temperature (35 °C limit after 6 h) under P0196 instead. GM does not use the code, and the code does not say which sensor or which system is at fault.

causes.label: Oil cooler (oil-to-coolant heat exchanger) clogged – oil much hotter than coolant
Engine module software (false setting, especially in cold weather)
Coolant or oil temperature sensor inaccurate, or its wiring faulty
Thermostat stuck open or low coolant
Block heater in use (only coolant preheated)

symptoms: Check engine light and/or wrench lamp (Ford)
Raised oil temperature with a clogged oil cooler
Often no driving symptoms when software is the cause

P0130.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0130.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0130 is the general circuit code, and manufacturers fill it very differently. Ford used it up to 2010 as the collective code for all wiring faults reported by the wide-band interface chip and has split it into specific codes since 2011. Subaru sets it when the interface voltages leave their range for 5 s, with immediate MIL. GM calls it 'closed loop performance': cross-talk from the heater (signal rises above 2 V with the heater off) or disagreement with the downstream sensor, two trips. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Wiring or connector of the bank 1 upstream sensor damaged, corroded or wet
Oxygen sensor faulty internally
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or mixture fault (plausibility versions)
Wrong or aftermarket sensor type
Control module or sensor interface chip faulty

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
Sensor and catalyst readiness not set

P0131.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0131.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. On switching sensors it means the signal stays below about 40–60 mV (GM, two trips; some GM engines also require the downstream sensor to read rich at the same time, since a genuinely lean mixture would show there too). On wide-band sensors (Ford from 2011, GM) it has nothing to do with the mixture: the interface chip reports one of the sensor wires shorted to ground. A really lean mixture leads to P0171/P2195 rather than this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Signal wire (or a wide-band sensor wire) shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on exhaust or gearbox
Sensor faulty or poisoned (permanently lean signal)
Large exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or misfires
Connector wet or corroded
Control module or interface chip faulty

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0132.title: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0132.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. On switching sensors the signal is above what the sensor can physically produce (about 1 V): Ford above 1.1 V for 10 s, GM above 1050 mV, Saab Trionic above 1.5 V for 5 s. The cause is almost always electrical – the heater supply or battery voltage on the signal wire, or a heater-to-signal short inside the sensor; some GM modules also read an open wire this way. On wide-band sensors the interface chip reports a sensor wire shorted to voltage. If P0132 and P0138 appear together, a shared short in the harness is likely. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to the heater supply or battery voltage (melted or chafed harness)
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire (GM reads its bias voltage)
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Sensor contaminated by silicone, coolant or oil

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly soot or fuel smell
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure
Often with P0138 or heater codes

P0133.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0133.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0133 means the sensor does not react fast enough to mixture changes. Methods differ fundamentally: GM measures passively how long the signal takes to cross 400–600 mV in each direction, averaged over 60 s; Ford forces the mixture to swing at 1.5 Hz and fails a switching sensor whose amplitude stays below 0.5 V, or evaluates response times of a wide-band sensor against a no-fault area; Subaru compares controller activity with measured lambda over 210 s. The test runs once per drive at warm part load; two trips. Mixture control usually stays active, but worse.

causes.label: Aged, sooted or poisoned upstream sensor (oil, silicone, coolant, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold gasket, crack)
Sensor heater weak or intermittent (sensor too cold)
Mixture fault: air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor
Wiring resistance or aftermarket sensor with different characteristics

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0134.title: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0134.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0134 means the sensor delivers no moving signal, typically because the circuit is open or the cell is cold or dead. The control module feeds a bias voltage, and that is all it sees: GM fails a signal stuck at 350–550 mV (or above 1700 mV with a 1.9 V bias) after warm-up, within about 15 s, or a cell resistance above 20 kΩ in hot exhaust; two trips. Subaru's wide-band sensor fails above 500 Ω cell impedance with immediate MIL. Ford's Bosch wide-band systems have used P2237 for this since 2011. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire, connector loose or corroded
Sensor faulty (cell high-resistance, worn out)
Sensor heater faulty – sensor does not get hot enough
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or cracked sensor
Control module bias or measuring circuit faulty

symptoms: No mixture control (open loop), higher consumption
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0135.title: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 1
P0135.description: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1) has an electric heater so that it reaches its working temperature of about 300 °C soon after a cold start. The control module switches the heater on the ground side and checks driver voltage and heater current: GM fails it outside 0.3–2.5 A (or 3.1 A) and calls it 'heater performance', Ford outside roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A, Saab Trionic outside 0.5–2.3 A for 5 s. Manufacturers split heater faults differently between P0030–P0032, P0053 and P0135. With the heater dead, closed-loop control starts late after a cold start. If P0135 and P0141 appear together, check the shared fuse.

causes.label: Heater element of the sensor burnt out (sensor must be replaced)
Fuse or relay of the heater supply faulty
Heater wiring or connector open, corroded or shorted
Unsuitable replacement sensor (different heater resistance)
Heater driver in the control module faulty

symptoms: Longer cold-start phase without mixture control, more fuel and emissions

P0136.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 2
P0136.description: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0136 is the general circuit code, and its exact meaning varies by manufacturer. Ford sets it as 'no activity' in a functional check: if the sensor never swings beyond about 0.42/0.48 V despite rich and lean phases – if needed after forced enrichment and leaning – once per drive cycle. Opel/GM Europe set it if the average voltage stays outside 400–500 mV after 10 min of closed loop; older Bosch Motronic if it stays at 0 V for 200 s despite heating. P0151.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0151.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0151 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0131. On switching sensors the signal stays below about 40–50 mV in closed loop with a stoichiometric target (GM LT4: 285 of 350 samples; GM 3.0/3.6 V6 within 50 s); on wide-band sensors the interface chip reports a sensor wire shorted to ground. Two trips. A genuinely lean bank 2 shows up as P0174 rather than this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Signal wire (or a wide-band sensor wire) shorted to ground, e.g. chafed on exhaust or gearbox
Sensor faulty or poisoned (permanently lean signal)
Large exhaust leak ahead of the sensor or misfires
Connector wet or corroded

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0152.title: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0152.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0152 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0132. Switching sensors: GM above 1050 mV (100 of 125 samples, after warm-up), Ford above 1.1 V for 10 s – a reading the sensor cannot produce itself, so heater or battery voltage on the signal wire is the usual cause; GM also reads an open wire as high. Wide-band sensors: a sensor wire shorted to voltage. P0152 together with P0158 points to a shared short in the bank 2 harness. Two trips. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to the heater supply or battery voltage (melted or chafed harness)
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire (GM reads its bias voltage)
Sensor contaminated by silicone, coolant or oil

symptoms: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)

P0153.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0153.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0153 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0133: the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes. GM measures passively the average response time in both directions across 300/400–600 mV over 60 s and also fails too few transitions; Ford modulates the mixture itself and evaluates amplitude, signal line length or response times. The test runs once per drive at warm part load, two trips. The previous obdex title of this code wrongly repeated P0152's 'High Voltage'.

causes.label: Aged, sooted or poisoned upstream sensor (oil, silicone, coolant, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold gasket, crack)
Sensor heater weak or intermittent (sensor too cold)
Mixture fault: air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor
Wiring resistance or aftermarket sensor with different characteristics

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0154.title: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0154.description: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. Bank 2 exists only on engines with two exhaust manifolds. P0154 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0134: the sensor delivers no moving signal and the control module only sees its own bias voltage. On GM's 3.0/3.6 V6 the code is set when the signal stays at 350–550 mV after heater warm-up, within about 15 s, in closed loop after 150 s of running; two trips. Ford's Bosch wide-band systems have used P2240 instead since 2011. A failed heater (P0155) can also lead to this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.

causes.label: Open or high-resistance signal or ground wire, connector loose or corroded
Sensor faulty (cell high-resistance, worn out)
Sensor heater faulty – sensor does not get hot enough
Control module bias or measuring circuit faulty

symptoms: No mixture control (open loop), higher consumption
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0155.title: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 1
P0155.description: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 (sensor 1) has its own electric heater. P0155 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0135: the heater current is outside its window or the driver voltage does not follow the command. GM fails it outside 0.3–3.1 A (8 s or 8 of 10 samples, two trips); Ford outside roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A, with related codes for heater temperature control (P0050) and resistance (P0059). Closed loop on bank 2 then starts late after a cold start, and the sensor checks are suspended. P0135 together with P0155 points to a shared supply or fuse.

causes.label: Heater element of the sensor burnt out (sensor must be replaced)
Fuse or relay of the heater supply faulty
Heater wiring or connector open, corroded or shorted
Heater driver in the control module faulty

symptoms: Higher emissions and consumption after cold start

P0156.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0156.description: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0156 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0136. Ford sets it as 'no activity' when the downstream sensor on bank 2 never swings outside a narrow band around 0.45 V in its functional check, if needed after forced mixture changes, once per drive cycle. Exhaust systems with a Y-pipe have only one downstream sensor, which counts as bank 1. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Downstream sensor aged or poisoned (stays in the middle band)
Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded
Sensor heater failed (sensor stays cold)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0157.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0157.description: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0157 means the signal stays below the lower limit, the bank 2 counterpart of P0137. GM sets it below 50 mV (two trips), on its 3.0 V6 within 50 s in closed loop; Ford uses its pull-up resistance check and counts both open circuit and short to ground as P0157. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground or melted against the exhaust
Sensor faulty (cracked element, thermal shock from water)
Signal circuit open (counts as low on Ford)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (lean reading)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0158.title: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0158.description: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. A zirconia sensor can hardly produce more than about 1 V, so readings above 1.05–1.15 V point to an outside voltage such as the heater supply on the signal wire; GM also sees an open circuit here because of its bias voltage. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Signal circuit open or high-resistance (GM bias logic)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0159.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0159.description: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. Bank 2 exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0159 means the downstream sensor on bank 2 reacts too slowly to mixture changes, typically measured around fuel cut-off. Thresholds are documented only for the bank 1 counterpart P0139 (Subaru: 0.51 s rich to lean, 2 s lean to rich); Jaguar Land Rover lists P0159 for its mid-cat sensor after water-induced thermal shock. Newer GM and Ford systems report direction-specific codes P013C/P013D and P014A/P014B instead. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Sensor aged or contaminated (oil ash, silicone, additives)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor heater weak, sensor too cold
Thermal shock damage from water

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)

P015A.title: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 1
P015A.description: The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late, or does not reach the target level at all, after the mixture has changed. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, usually tested during deceleration fuel cut-off. GM uses this on switching (narrow-band) sensors: while the fuel cut-off for the downstream tests is running, it measures how long the upstream sensor takes to start dropping from above 680 mV and fails a filtered delay above about 0.58 s after one trip. Conditions include warm engine, 40–78 mph and a hot converter. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).

causes.label: Upstream oxygen sensor aged or poisoned (silicone, oil, coolant, soot)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold, flange)
Mixture fault: intake air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor
Sensor heater weak, sensor too cold
Connector, wiring or control module software

symptoms: Slightly higher consumption or rough idle possible
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P015B.title: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Lean to Rich Bank 1 Sensor 1
P015B.description: The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late, or does not reach the target level at all, after the mixture has changed. This code covers the lean-to-rich direction, tested when fuel returns or the control module briefly enriches the mixture. GM measures the upstream switching sensor's delay while the mixture is enriched for the downstream tests and fails a filtered delay above about 0.58 s (fallback 1.9 s) after one trip; the test needs the rich-to-lean counterpart P015A completed first. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).

causes.label: Upstream oxygen sensor aged or poisoned (silicone, oil, coolant, soot)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (manifold, flange)
Mixture fault: intake air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor
Sensor heater weak, sensor too cold
Connector, wiring or control module software

Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P015C.title: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 2 Sensor 1
P015C.description: The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late, or does not reach the target level at all, after the mixture has changed. GM documents it for switching sensors with a bank 2 limit of about 0.60 s (filtered) and 2.0 s as fallback, set after one trip during the forced fuel cut-off. Connector, wiring or control module software

P015D.title: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Lean to Rich Bank 2 Sensor 1
P015D.description: The upstream oxygen sensor (sensor 1, before the catalytic converter) is the main control sensor for the air-fuel mixture. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late, or does not reach the target level at all, after the mixture has changed. Mixture fault: intake air leak, injectors, fuel pressure, air flow sensor

Connector, wiring or control module software
