Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P015E.title: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Fuel Timing Control
P015E.description: Diesel fuel systems correct injection timing and quantity in closed loop, often with learning routines that run during suitable overrun phases. CARB requires a fault when such feedback control does not start within a manufacturer-defined time. P015E is the code of this kind for injection timing control: the closed-loop correction does not become active in time, or does not learn. It belongs to a family of similar codes – Ford's 2023 diesels, for example, set the sister code P016D when rail pressure adaptation has learned nothing after 300 s. No manufacturer document describing P015E itself, or its threshold, was found; the description rests on CARB and the sister code. Frequent causes are learning conditions that occur too rarely, software, or injectors outside tolerance.

causes.label: Learning conditions (overrun phases, temperatures) met too rarely
Control module software
Injectors outside tolerance or unstable fuel pressure
Injector wiring or sensors faulty
Engine control module faulty

symptoms: Possibly louder combustion noise or uneven running with unlearned injectors

P015F.title: Excessive Time to Enter Closed Loop Cylinder Balance Control
P015F.description: Cylinder balance control evens out the contribution of individual cylinders – on diesels by adjusting each injector's quantity based on crankshaft speed fluctuations. P015F, by its title, is set when this closed-loop control does not become active within the expected time after starting, for example because the crankshaft wheel has not been learned or the conditions are missing. No manufacturer using P015F was found: Ford's 2023 diesels run cylinder balancing (maximum correction 3.5–15 mg per stroke) but report problems as P0263–P0284. The description therefore rests on CARB's requirement for feedback controls and that comparable function; causes are derived, not documented.

causes.label: Crankshaft wheel adaptation not learned or speed signal disturbed
Injector deviating strongly or injector circuit fault
Control module software

P0160.title: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0160.description: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 2 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor used for converter monitoring and downstream mixture trim; it exists only on V and boxer engines with a separate downstream sensor per bank. P0160 means the sensor shows no change in voltage although it is heated and the engine is in closed loop; the control module only sees its own bias voltage, so the circuit is open or high-resistance or the sensor is dead. On GM's 3.0/3.6 V6 the code sets within 15 s after more than 150 s of running; newer GM systems apply 1900 mV and treat above 1700 mV as open; two trips. Ford does not use P0160 and reports 'no activity' as P0156. A failed heater (P0161) can also cause it. The previous obdex title mixed in 'Slow Response', which is P0159. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Signal or ground wire open or high-resistance, connector corroded
Sensor dead, poisoned or damaged by thermal shock
Heater failed or fuse blown by a heater short
Signal wire shorted to voltage

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness for bank 2 not set

P0161.title: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 2
P0161.description: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 (sensor 2) has an electric heater so that it reaches working temperature quickly. P0161 concerns this heater circuit and its performance. GM measures the current through its low-side driver and fails it outside 0.3–2.9 A on the supercharged V8 (8 of 10 samples, two trips). Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the current once per drive cycle once the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C; the lower limit is 0.22–0.55 A depending on sensor type, the upper 3 A. Without heat the sensor becomes active late or not at all, so P0159/P0160 can follow; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Heater element of the sensor burnt out
Heater wiring, connector or fuse open or corroded
Short in the heater circuit (current too high)
Driver in the engine module faulty

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness for bank 2 not set

P0162.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0162.description: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0162 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0142. Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. The previous obdex titles from P0162 to P0165 were shifted by one position; P0162 had carried the heater title of P0161. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Sensor faulty or damaged by thermal shock
Wiring or connector under the car damaged
Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover)
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0163.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0163.description: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0163 means the signal stays close to 0 V – typically the signal wire is shorted to ground; on some modules an open circuit is also reported this way, and an exhaust leak ahead of the sensor can make it read lean. For the bank 2 sensor 2 counterpart GM uses below 50 mV within 50 s, Ford a pull-up resistance check (short below 10 Ω, open above 1 MΩ). Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafed or melted)
Sensor faulty
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor (apparently lean)
Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0164.title: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0164.description: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0164 means the signal is above about 1.05–1.15 V. A switching sensor can produce at most about 1 V, so anything higher is electrical: a short to voltage or to the heater wire, or – on GM's bias logic – an open ground. Ford's over-voltage test (above 1.1 V for 10 s) explicitly covers downstream sensors 2 and 3. Jaguar Land Rover assigns the code to that sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes; no thresholds are published for sensor 3, so the logic follows the sensor 2 checks. When it fails, the downstream evaluation of that converter is suspended; there is no limp mode.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to voltage or to the heater wire
Sensor faulty internally (heater-to-signal short)
Sensor ground open (GM logic)
Engine module software (Jaguar Land Rover)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0165.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0165.description: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. Wiring or connector high-resistance

P0166.title: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0166.description: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0167.title: O2 Sensor Heater Circuit Bank 2 Sensor 3
P0167.description: Sensor 3 on bank 2 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick. It is rare – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (2013–2016), where it is the 'post-cat' sensor of the second bank, and for Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0167 concerns its heater. Ford checks the driver voltage continuously and the heater current once per drive cycle when the sensor is estimated above about 120 °C and has heated for 30 s; below 0.22–0.55 A (depending on sensor type) or above 3 A is a fault, and the heater resistance has its own code (P0061). causes.label: Heater element burnt out

Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0168.title: Fuel Temperature Too High
P0168.description: P0168 is not a sensor fault but an operating condition, almost only on diesels: the fuel temperature sensor reports fuel hotter than a protective limit. The fuel heats up through the return flow from the high-pressure pump and injectors, especially with little fuel in the tank, at idle after full load, in hot weather or with a failed fuel cooler; one manufacturer patent names about 80 °C as the upper limit to protect seals, against a normal range of roughly 5–60 °C. On Saab's Bosch EDC16 diesels the code means an engine protection function is active and injection quantity is reduced. No manufacturer threshold was found, and GM's and Ford's diesel summaries do not use P0168. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the manufacturer.

causes.label: Fuel cooler (air or water cooler in the return) dirty or faulty, coolant circuit disturbed
Very little fuel in the tank at high load or heat
Excessive return flow from worn high-pressure pump or injectors, or faulty overflow valve
Fuel temperature sensor drifting and reading too high
Engine overheating or overload (trailer, gradient)

symptoms: Loss of power, limp mode (reduced injection quantity)
Occurs in heat, at full load, with little fuel in the tank

P0169.title: Incorrect Fuel Composition
P0169.description: According to its title, P0169 means the control module has detected a fuel composition outside what is expected – wrong fuel or an impermissible ethanol or water content – while the composition sensor itself works. None of the manufacturer OBD documents checked (GM, Ford) uses the code: GM reports water or conductive fuel via the ethanol sensor frequency as P2269, and Ford has had no composition sensor since 2000. Claims that diesel makers use it for misfuelling or water could not be verified. The description therefore rests on CARB, which lists the fuel composition sensor as a monitored component, and on component information. Unrecognised fuel usually also shows up as mixture adaptation codes.

causes.label: Wrong fuel (E85 in a non-flex-fuel vehicle, ethanol content outside calibration)
Water or contamination in the fuel
Fuel composition sensor drifting (value in range but wrong)
Control module software

symptoms: Poor cold start, stumbling, loss of power

P016A.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control
P016A.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. Closed loop needs a heated, working oxygen sensor and plausible engine data. P016A means the mixture control did not switch to closed loop within the calibrated time after starting; the engine then runs on map values with higher emissions but no actual limp mode. CARB requires this check, and since 2019 also after every automatic restart in start-stop systems. Bentley and other VW group petrol engines set it together with oxygen sensor heater codes when the heater fuse holder was damaged; Ram's 3.0 EcoDiesel listed it in bulletins fixed with new software and sensors. Time limits are not public.

causes.label: Oxygen sensor heater not working (fuse, fuse holder, wiring, heater element)
Oxygen sensor sluggish or aged
Control module software (false setting)
Engine not warming up (thermostat open, coolant sensor)

symptoms: Often with oxygen sensor or heater codes

P016B.title: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Rich
P016B.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016B means the mixture control as a whole has reached its lower limit: it already removes as much fuel as allowed and the mixture is still rich. In substance it matches P0172, but without a bank reference – for manufacturers whose strategy evaluates the control loop as a whole. CARB requires a fault once the adaptation has used up its range. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; Hyundai documents the lean counterpart P016C. Typical causes are those of a rich mixture: excessive fuel pressure, leaking injectors or an open purge valve.

causes.label: Fuel pressure too high / high-pressure pump or regulator fault (direct injection)
Leaking injectors
Purge valve open
Oxygen sensor or air flow/pressure sensor offset, control module software

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P016C.title: Closed Loop Air/Fuel Ratio Control At Limit - System Too Lean
P016C.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P016C means the mixture control as a whole has reached its upper limit: it already adds as much fuel as allowed and still cannot reach lambda 1. In substance it matches P0171, without a bank reference. Hyundai documents it on the 2021 Elantra 2.0: if the fuel adaptation was learned wrongly after starts below −10 °C, the engine could stall when stopping or at idle and set P016C; new engine software changed the learning logic. Otherwise the usual lean causes apply: air leaks, low fuel delivery or an air flow sensor reading low.

causes.label: Air leak (intake, crankcase ventilation)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low
Wrongly learned adaptation / control module software
Air flow or pressure sensor reading low, injectors clogged

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Stalling when stopping or at idle

P016D.title: Excessive Time To Enter Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control
P016D.description: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016D means the pressure control has not settled into closed loop, or has not learned, in the time allowed. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) set it when, within the learning conditions – target rail pressure 600–1300 bar, fuel at most 40 °C – no new adaptation factor has been learned after 300 s; the check only runs while the rail pressure sensor and its supply are fault-free. Ford reports adaptation at its limit separately as P228E/P228F. Use on petrol engines was not found. Often there are no noticeable symptoms.

causes.label: Rail pressure sensor drifting (wrong slope)
Volume or pressure control valve sticking or worn
Unstable low-pressure supply (filter, lift pump, air in system)
Fuel leak or high injector return flow
Control module software

symptoms: Occasional power reduction or rough idle

P016E.title: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too High
P016E.description: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016E means the controller is already at its limit in the 'reduce pressure' direction and the measured pressure is still above target. That can be real overpressure – a control valve that lets too much through or a blocked return – or a falsely high reading. Volvo and Mack document P016E on their 11 and 13 litre truck diesels together with P0194, caused by corroded contacts at the rail pressure sensor; the fix is a new sensor and internal harness. No public thresholds exist; Ford reports the comparable condition as P228F. Use on passenger-car diesels or petrol engines was not documented.

causes.label: Rail pressure sensor or its contacts/wiring (corrosion) giving a falsely high signal
Pressure or volume control valve sticking (lets too much through)
Return line from control valve or rail blocked or kinked
Control module software or calibration

P016F.title: Closed Loop Fuel Pressure Control At Limit - Pressure Too Low
P016F.description: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016F means the controller is at its limit in the 'more pressure' direction and the actual pressure still stays below target. Which circuit is meant depends on the manufacturer: Volvo and Mack use it for rail pressure, for example as a follow-up when their electronic pressure relief valve stays open (P009B); on FCA's 3.0 EcoDiesel it concerns the regulated low-pressure supply via the fuel pump control module and appears with P025C and P01C6, partly fixed by new engine software. No public thresholds exist. Weak supply pumps, clogged filters and corroded connectors or grounds are typical causes.

causes.label: Weak low-pressure supply: lift/tank pump, pump control module, clogged filter
Connector or ground problems (corrosion, water) at pump module, low-pressure sensor or ground point
Pressure relief valve open or its control circuit interrupted
Worn high-pressure pump or internal leak
Engine control module software

symptoms: Hard starting, long cranking, stalling after start

P0170.title: Fuel Trim Bank 1
P0170.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0170 is the older, direction-neutral code for 'mixture adaptation of bank 1 out of range'; whether lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. Users are Mercedes-Benz petrol engines, which often set P0170/P0173 instead of P0171–P0175 – a Mercedes-Benz magazine for independent workshops reports that cleaning or replacing the air flow sensor most often cures it – and Ford's 6.7 litre diesel, where it flags a fuel quantity error above 15 % in either direction from its fuel mass observer. GM and Ford petrol engines do not use it. Two trips.

causes.label: Air flow sensor dirty or drifting
Air leak or crankcase ventilation leaking
Injection quantity error (diesel: injector drift, rail pressure sensor; petrol: injectors, fuel pressure)
Oxygen or NOx sensor offset

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P0171.title: System Too Lean Bank 1
P0171.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0171 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its upper limit: the module already adds the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays lean. GM sets it at a long-term factor of about 1.30–1.36 (+30–36 %, engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; it needs two trips and is suspended during heavy purge flow or intrusive tests. GM bulletins repeatedly trace it to leaking crankcase ventilation hoses or pipes on V6 and V8 engines; Ford found leaking direct injectors. P0171 together with P0174 points to a shared cause. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause.

causes.label: Air leak after the air flow sensor (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick)
Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty)
Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling
Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating
Hissing or whistling from the engine bay (air leak, PCV)

P0172.title: System Too Rich Bank 1
P0172.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0172 means long-term trim on bank 1 is at its lower limit: the module already removes the maximum fuel and the mixture still stays rich. GM separates purge influence carefully: before the first purge it evaluates passively (factor 0.70 or below, i.e. −30 %), afterwards it closes the purge valve briefly for an active test, so a full charcoal canister is not counted as a fault. Ford only evaluates with purge off, at −25 %. Two trips. Bulletins name an open purge valve, leaking direct injectors and, on flex-fuel vehicles, a wrongly learned ethanol content. A permanently rich mixture can overheat the converter and dilutes the oil.

causes.label: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated
Leaking or dripping injectors (also direct injection)
Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose)
Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation
Clogged air filter or intake, air flow sensor reading high; flex-fuel: wrongly learned ethanol content

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough idle or starting problems after refuelling; converter damage possible later

P0173.title: Fuel Trim Bank 2
P0173.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0173 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0170: a direction-neutral trim fault, so whether bank 2 runs lean or rich has to be read from the trim values. It is mainly used by Mercedes-Benz V6 and V8 petrol engines instead of P0174/P0175; their workshop magazine names the air flow sensor as the most frequent fix. P0170 and P0173 together point to a common cause. No manufacturer threshold was found; the description rests on CARB's fuel system monitoring requirement and that publication. Two trips.

causes.label: Air flow sensor dirty or faulty
Air leak on bank 2 or at the crankcase ventilation
Fuel pressure or bank 2 injectors
Exhaust leak ahead of the bank 2 oxygen sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P0174.title: System Too Lean Bank 2
P0174.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0174 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0171 and only exists on V and boxer engines with separate mixture control per bank. The limits match: GM a long-term factor of about 1.30 (engine-specific), Ford above +25 % with short-term trim above +1 %; an older Saab V6 flagged more than 25 % deviation for 20 s. Two trips, no limp mode. P0174 alone points to a leak, injector or exhaust leak on bank 2; together with P0171 to a shared cause such as the air flow sensor, fuel pressure or crankcase ventilation – exactly what several GM bulletins describe. Diagnosis hint: trims very high only at idle and normal under load point to an air leak; trims rising with load point to fuel shortage or an air flow sensor reading low. The oxygen sensor only reports what is in the exhaust and is rarely the cause.

causes.label: Air leak after the air flow sensor on bank 2 (intake manifold gasket, vacuum hoses, throttle body gasket, brake booster line)
Crankcase ventilation leaking or faulty (PCV hose, diaphragm in valve cover, oil cap, dipstick)
Air flow sensor dirty or drifting (measures too little air)
Fuel pressure or delivery too low (weak pump, clogged filter, regulator, tank nearly empty)
Injectors clogged, or exhaust leak ahead of the oxygen sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough or unsteady idle, possibly stalling
Hesitation or lack of power when accelerating
Hissing or whistling from the engine bay (air leak, PCV)

P0175.title: System Too Rich Bank 2
P0175.description: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. P0175 is the bank 2 counterpart of P0172: long-term trim at its lower limit, mixture still rich. GM evaluates it like bank 1 with a passive test before the first purge and an active test with the purge valve closed; Ford at −25 % with purge off. Two trips, no limp mode. P0175 alone points to a bank-specific cause such as a leaking injector on bank 2; together with P0172 to fuel pressure, purge, ethanol learning on flex-fuel vehicles or fuel in the oil. GM and Ford bulletins document wrongly learned ethanol content and a purge valve stuck open as causes.

causes.label: Purge valve stuck open or charcoal canister saturated
Leaking or dripping injectors on bank 2 (also direct injection)
Fuel pressure too high (faulty regulator, blocked return, regulator vacuum hose)
Fuel in the engine oil (short trips, leaking injectors), vapour via crankcase ventilation

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Rough idle or starting problems after refuelling; converter damage possible later

P0176.title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit
P0176.description: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0176 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. GM's current documents use P0178/P0179 instead, so P0176 is mainly to be expected on older flex-fuel vehicles or other makes. GM issued a special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models (10 years/150,000 miles) because road salt could make the sensor fail electrically, turning on the MIL and disabling remote start. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information.

causes.label: Flex-fuel sensor electrically failed (corrosion from road salt)
Connector or wire corroded, open or shorted
Supply (relay, fuse) missing
Engine control module

symptoms: Ethanol content in scan data implausible or frozen

P0177.title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0177.description: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0177 means the signal lies within the valid frequency range but is implausible – it jumps, changes without a refuelling event or does not match the mixture adaptation. Such sensors measure permittivity, conductivity and temperature and compare them with tables of known blends. GM's documents only list low, high and P2269, so no manufacturer threshold for P0177 was found; the description rests on CARB's rationality requirement and component information.

causes.label: Sensor drifting or dirty inside
Water or contamination in the fuel
Loose contact in the connector
Control module or software

symptoms: Wrong ethanol value, stumbling or starting problems

P0178.title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit Low
P0178.description: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0178 means the frequency is too low. GM sets it below 45 Hz with 50 of 63 samples failing at 100 ms intervals (about 6 s), monitored continuously with the powertrain relay above 11 V; two trips. 'Low' refers to the frequency, not to the ethanol content: an open wire, missing supply or short to ground gives 0 Hz. The control module then uses a learned or substitute ethanol value. GM's road-salt special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models concerns exactly this kind of electrical failure.

causes.label: Signal wire open or shorted to ground
Sensor without supply (relay, fuse, ground)
Sensor electrically failed (corrosion)
Engine control module

P0179.title: Fuel Composition Sensor Circuit High
P0179.description: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0179 means the frequency is above the physically possible range for E100 plus tolerance. GM sets it between 155 and 185 Hz (50 of 63 samples, two trips); above 185 Hz it sets P2269 instead, because such a high value indicates water or conductive fuel rather than a sensor fault. Typical causes of P0179 are failed sensor electronics or interference on the signal wire. With a falsely high ethanol value the mixture tends to run rich.

causes.label: Sensor electronics faulty
Interference or short on the signal wire
Water or conductive fuel near the P2269 limit
Engine control module

P017A.title: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P017A.description: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017A is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found: VW uses P017B/P017C/P017E for its sensor, and Ford's summaries list its own codes. Ford's published summaries still use its own codes P1289/P1290 for this sensor (fault below 0.244 V or above 4.96 V for 5 s). The description rests on CARB and component information. On a sensor fault the control module typically uses a modelled temperature and runs the radiator fan.

causes.label: Wiring or connector open or corroded
Sensor faulty (moisture in the housing)
Engine control module

symptoms: Coolant temperature warning or wrong gauge reading
Radiator fan runs loud or constantly

P017B.title: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P017B.description: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017B means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – for example it does not fit other temperature sensors after a long standstill or does not rise as expected. Audi documents it on 2019–2021 V8 TFSI models and Bentley on V8 models from 2018 onwards, together with a cooling system fault code and a red coolant warning: a damaged O-ring at the sensor tip lets water into the housing and damages the sensing element, often intermittently; the fix is a new sender. GM lists P017B only as an exclusion condition in its diesel software. Thresholds are not public.

causes.label: Sensor damaged by moisture (O-ring)
Genuine temperature problem (air in cooling system, thermostat)
Contact resistance at the connector
Software or calibration

symptoms: Red coolant warning or overheating warning
Radiator fan runs loud or constantly

P017C.title: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P017C.description: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017C means the signal voltage is too low – a short to ground of the signal wire or a short inside the sensor; the control module would read an implausibly hot cylinder head. 'Low' refers to the signal, not the temperature. Audi and Bentley document it as a short to ground, most often caused by water inside sender G407 after O-ring damage. Ford flags the same condition on its own code below 0.244 V for 5 s. A substitute value is used; an overheating warning with a cold engine is a typical sign.

causes.label: Water or coolant inside the sensor (O-ring damaged)
Signal wire chafed against ground
Sensor shorted internally
Engine control module

symptoms: Overheating or coolant warning despite a cold engine

P017D.title: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P017D.description: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017D means the signal voltage is too high – the sensor or wire is open or shorted to voltage, and the control module would read an implausibly cold head. Ford's published summaries flag this under its own code P1289 above 4.96 V for 5 s, but a 2019 bulletin for the F-150 and Mustang 5.0 litre names P1289 and/or P017D and replaces the sensor – so at least that calibration also sets the generic code. GM lists P017D only as an exclusion condition in its diesel software. The engine uses substitute values; the radiator fan typically runs constantly.

causes.label: Sensor faulty (series fault on Ford 5.0 litre 2019)
Connector unplugged or corroded, wire open
Signal wire shorted to voltage
Engine control module

P017E.title: Cylinder Head Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P017E.description: The cylinder head temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor that measures the temperature of the cylinder head metal or of the coolant in the head. Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. CARB requires such sensors to be monitored like the coolant sensor. P017E covers intermittent interruptions or an erratic signal. The VW group explicitly uses it for 'open circuit or loose contact', not only for jumps: on Audi and Bentley V8 engines moisture inside sender G407 after O-ring damage makes it fail intermittently, and an improved part has been introduced. Loose contacts and wires broken by heat or engine movement are other causes. The detection logic is not public.

causes.label: Moisture inside the sensor (O-ring)
Loose contact at connector or pin
Wire broken by engine movement or heat
Sensor faulty internally

P017F.title: EVAP System Leak Detection Pump Module Air Filter Restricted
P017F.description: Leak detection pump modules in the evaporative emission system (for example Bosch's DM-TL, used by VW, BMW, Porsche, Volvo, Mini, Land Rover and Kia/Hyundai) draw fresh air through their own filter, often mounted separately via a hose; at rest the charcoal canister is also vented through it. P017F means this filter is restricted – by dust, mud or water when fitted near a wheel arch. The reference measurement of the pump and the venting are then distorted, and the tank can pull a vacuum. A GM patent describes detection via the pressure difference across the filter during purge (above about 8 inH2O for 10–20 s). No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's requirement to monitor evaporative system components and these component sources.

causes.label: Leak detection pump filter dirty or blocked
Moisture or ice in filter or hose
Hose between filter and pump kinked or blocked
Pump module faulty (wrong reference)

symptoms: Usually no noticeable change in driving

P0180.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0180.description: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0180 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. None of the manufacturers checked (GM, Ford, Saab/Bosch, Nissan) uses it – they report P0181–P0184 instead. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information. With a sensor fault the control module uses a substitute temperature (Saab EDC16: 50 °C).

causes.label: Wire or connector open or corroded
Sensor faulty
Control module reference or ground

symptoms: Substitute value; possibly starting problems in cold or hot conditions

P0181.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0181.description: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0181 is the plausibility check: after a long standstill fuel temperature must be close to another temperature sensor. Ford's 2023 diesels compare it after 6 h with the charge air cooler outlet temperature (limit 40 °C, or 20 °C without a block heater); GM diesels compare it after 8 h with a reference sensor (20 °C, two trips). Bulletins show other causes: Ford may set P0181 during a running self-test with fuel below 10 °C and warns against replacing parts without a confirmed fault; Nissan Rogues set it because of misrouted wires at the pump unit; Ford's 2018 6.7 diesel needed new software.

causes.label: Sensor drifting (characteristic shifted)
Comparison sensor wrong (charge air, coolant, intake air)
Block heater or unusual temperatures (cold fuel during self-test)
Wiring or connector (e.g. routing at the pump unit)
Control module software

symptoms: Check engine light on (often without change in driving)
Possibly harder cold or hot start
Diesel: less accurate rail pressure and quantity correction

P0182.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0182.description: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0182 means the signal is below its valid range – with an NTC that points to a short to ground or an internally shorted sensor, and the control module would read about 150 °C. Limits: Ford diesel below 0.095 V, Ford petrol below 0.12 V for 5 s, GM diesel below 50 Ω (two trips), GM 6.6 litre below 0.60 V for 5 s, Saab EDC16 below 0.23 V for 0.6 s with a substitute value of 50 °C. Genuinely hot fuel within the valid range is P0168 instead.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing)
Sensor shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Engine control module

symptoms: Fuel temperature in scan data implausibly high (about 150 °C)

P0183.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0183.description: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0183 means the signal is above its valid range – typically an open circuit, an unplugged connector, an open sensor ground or a short to 5 V; the control module would read about −40 °C. Limits: Ford diesel above 4.92 V, Ford petrol above 4.82 V for 5 s, GM diesel above about 122 kΩ (two trips), GM 6.6 litre above 4.71 V for 5 s, Saab EDC16 above 4.96 V for 0.6 s. On the Nissan Rogue the sensor sits in the fuel pump unit in the tank, and misrouted wires there caused P0183/P0181.

causes.label: Connector off or wire open
Sensor open internally
Wiring routing or chafing at the pump unit
Sensor ground open or short to 5 V
Engine control module

symptoms: Fuel temperature in scan data about −40 °C
Usually no change in driving; possibly hot-start problems

P0184.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent
P0184.description: Fuel temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. P0184 covers jumps in the signal: fuel cannot heat up or cool down that fast, so a sudden change points to a loose contact. GM diesels check every new value against an exponentially filtered window around the last good value and set the code when 10 of 15 samples (100 ms each) fall outside; two trips, blocked while a circuit fault is active. GM still writes 'Circuit Intermittent' in 2016 and 2018 – a change to 'Intermittent/Erratic' is not documented. No source was found for petrol engines.

causes.label: Loose contact or weak terminal tension in the connector
Wire break or chafing from vibration
Sensor with internal dropouts
Corrosion from moisture

symptoms: Fuel temperature in scan data jumps

P0185.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor B Circuit
P0185.description: Fuel temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. Sensor B is the second measuring point, for example GM's 6.6 litre diesel sensor 2 or a second rail. P0185 is the general circuit fault of this sensor, the counterpart of P0180. None of the manufacturers checked uses it; GM reports sensor 2 faults as P0187/P0188. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information.

causes.label: Wire or connector open or corroded
Sensor faulty
Control module reference or ground

symptoms: Substitute value, usually no change in driving

P0186.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0186.description: Fuel temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. Sensor B is the second measuring point, for example GM's 6.6 litre diesel sensor 2 or a second rail. P0186 is the plausibility check of sensor B, the counterpart of P0181 – presumably a comparison with a reference sensor after a long standstill, as GM documents for sensor A (8 h, 20 °C). No manufacturer using P0186 was found; the description rests on CARB and the sensor A strategy.

causes.label: Sensor drifting (characteristic shifted)
Comparison sensor wrong (charge air, coolant, intake air)
Contact resistance in the connector

P0187.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low
P0187.description: Fuel temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. On diesels it sits in the injection pump, rail or return line; on Ford petrol direct-injection engines it is built into the rail pressure sensor, and GM uses digital rail temperature sensors on its direct-injection engines. Sensor B is the second measuring point, for example GM's 6.6 litre diesel sensor 2 or a second rail. P0187 means the signal of sensor B is below its valid range – with an analogue NTC a short to ground or very hot reading. GM's 6.6 litre diesel sets it below 0.60 V (above about 150 °C) for 5 s; GM's direct-injection petrol engines use a digital rail temperature sensor 2 and set it below a count of 145 in 50 of 62 samples, two trips – communication faults of these digital sensors have codes of their own.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground (chafing)
Sensor shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Engine control module

symptoms: Implausibly high fuel temperature in scan data

causes.label: Connector off or wire open
Sensor open internally
Sensor ground open or short to 5 V
Engine control module

symptoms: Fuel temperature about −40/−50 °C in scan data

P0189.title: Fuel Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent
P0189.description: Fuel temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor: the hotter the fuel, the lower its resistance and signal voltage. causes.label: Loose contact or weak terminal tension in the connector
Wire break or chafing from vibration
Sensor with internal dropouts

P018A.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P018A.description: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). Sensor A is the high-pressure rail sensor (P0190–P0194). P018A is the general circuit fault for when a manufacturer does not distinguish low from high. GM and Ford, whose sensor B functions are documented, use P018C/P018D instead, so no manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and the component information. When the sensor fails, the control module uses a pre-set value and usually runs the supply pump with fixed control.

causes.label: Connector corroded or loose, broken wire
Sensor faulty
5 V reference disturbed (shared with other sensors)
Engine or fuel pump control module, or CAN transmission

symptoms: Often no noticeable change in driving
Starting problems or hesitation with fixed pump control

P018B.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P018B.description: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). Sensor A is the high-pressure rail sensor (P0190–P0194). P018B is the plausibility fault. GM checks actively whether the sensor responds: if the pump duty sits at its limit for 5 s or the pressure error varies too little, the module changes pump output and fails the sensor if pressure moves 30 kPa or less – a 'frozen' sensor; two trips. Ford checks the deviation from target instead: more than 20 psi (about 1.4 bar) for 8 s with a plausible target of 35–60 psi, which can also be a genuine pressure problem. A fault-free P018B is a precondition for GM's pump output check (P2635) and Ford's supply checks (P008A/P008B).

causes.label: Sensor drifting or stuck (diaphragm, electronics)
Genuine low-pressure fault: weak pump, clogged filter, faulty regulator
Contact resistance at connector or ground
Fuel pump control module or its control

symptoms: Hard starting or hesitation when accelerating

P018C.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P018C.description: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). Sensor A is the high-pressure rail sensor (P0190–P0194). P018C means the signal voltage is below its lower limit – a signal wire shorted to ground, or an open signal or 5 V reference wire; a short on another sensor sharing the reference can also pull it down. GM sets it below 4 % of the reference (about 0.2 V), or below 0.14 V when the sensor is read by the fuel pump module, in 64 or 72 of 80 samples; two trips. Ford sets it below 0.049 V for 8 s. The control module then uses a fixed value or fixed pump control.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground or open
5 V reference missing or shorted (also by another sensor on the circuit)
Sensor faulty
Connector corroded

P018D.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P018D.description: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). Water ingress in the connector is a common trigger. A substitute value is used.

causes.label: Sensor ground open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Sensor faulty
Connector corrosion or water ingress

P018E.title: Fuel Pressure Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P018E.description: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). Sensor A is the high-pressure rail sensor (P0190–P0194). P018E covers a signal that jumps faster than real pressure can change or drops out briefly without staying low or high – typically a loose contact or chafed wire; on GM-style systems where the pump module sends the value over CAN, a disturbed transmission is also possible. GM and Ford do not use this code in the documents checked, so no manufacturer thresholds were found; the description rests on CARB and component information.

causes.label: Loose contact or connector corrosion
Chafed harness
Sensor faulty internally
CAN transmission from the pump module disturbed

P018F.title: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Frequent Activation
P018F.description: Common-rail diesels have a pressure relief valve in the rail – usually a spring-loaded valve, on some truck engines electronically controlled. It opens on overpressure and then holds a low limp-home pressure; every opening wears the seat, and after many openings it may no longer close tightly. P018F means the valve has opened too often: the control module recognises openings from the rail pressure trace (overshoot, then a steep drop to the limp-home level) and counts them. The code therefore usually points to an underlying problem – the pressure control repeatedly lets overpressure build up. No manufacturer document describing P018F was found; the function and counting logic come from patents on large engines (example: opening at about 1950 bar, then about 800 bar).

causes.label: Volume control valve sticking – repeated overpressure
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong (controller targets too high)
Relief valve fatigued, opening too early
Return blocked or pressure control valve faulty
Load changes or overrun steps with software faults

symptoms: Sudden loss of power (limp mode with low rail pressure)
Starting problems once the valve no longer seals
Smoke or harsh combustion noise beforehand

P0190.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit
P0190.description: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines – a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference. P0190 is the general circuit code used when a manufacturer does not split low and high; GM and Ford use P0192/P0193 instead. Bosch EDC16 diesels (Saab/Opel 1.9) report P0190 with a fault type byte, and a Saab bulletin traces it to corrosion in the sensor connector, sometimes with no restart for up to 15 minutes. On a sensor fault the engine runs on a calculated pressure in limp mode – on Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel with at most 40 MPa rail pressure and 20 % pedal.

causes.label: Connector corroded or water ingress at the rail pressure sensor
Rail pressure sensor faulty
Harness damaged (heat, chafing)
5 V reference disturbed

symptoms: Stalling or no start (sometimes only after a waiting time)

P0191.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0191.description: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0191 means the signal is electrically valid but not believable – stuck, offset or drifting. Manufacturers check it differently: Ford's 2023 diesels and GM's diesels test the offset with the system depressurised (Ford before starting after 10 min and 12 s after switch-off, window about 0.25–0.38 V; GM 6.5–14 % of supply); GM petrol direct injection compares the two SENT channels (limit 1.0 MPa); Saab's V6 diesel flags a large target deviation while the signal barely moves. GM treats it as a one-trip fault. Ford petrol direct injection uses P0087/P0088 instead. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.

causes.label: Rail pressure sensor drifting or stuck (wrong offset at 0 bar)
Genuine pressure fault: high-pressure pump, pressure or volume control valve, tank pump
Connector corroded, contact resistance in signal or ground
Fuel shortage or clogged filter
Control module software

P0192.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low
P0192.description: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0192 means the signal is below the physically possible range – typically a signal wire shorted to ground or an open 5 V reference. Limits: Ford diesel below 0.13 V for 0.5 s, Ford petrol direct injection below 0.20 V for 5 s, GM diesel below 4.3 % of supply, GM 6.6 litre below 0.19 V, Saab/GM 2.0 diesel below 0.25 V. On a fault the module uses a substitute value and usually limits power.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground, harness chafed
5 V reference open or shorted
Connector corroded or loose
Rail pressure sensor faulty internally
Engine control module

P0193.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit High
P0193.description: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0193 means the signal is above its valid range – typically an open sensor ground or a short to voltage; where the module uses a pull-up on the signal line (Saab/GM 2.0 diesel), an open signal wire also reads 5 V and sets P0193. Limits: Ford diesel above 3.17 V (its sensor stays well below that even at maximum pressure), Ford petrol direct injection above 4.80 V for 5 s, GM above about 95 % of supply, Saab above 4.7 V. causes.label: Sensor ground open or high-resistance
Signal wire open (with pull-up) or shorted to voltage
Connector corroded
Sensor faulty
Engine control module

P0194.title: Fuel Rail Pressure Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0194.description: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0194 detects jumps or dropouts: the signal changes faster than rail pressure physically can. Volvo/Mack bulletins trace it to corroded or worn contacts at sensor and harness, often together with P016E because the pressure control reacts to the jumping signal; the fix was a new sensor and harness section.

causes.label: Corrosion or wear at sensor and harness contacts
Harness chafed or loose contact
Rail pressure sensor faulty internally
Ground problem or control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (not on GM 2016 diesels)
Occasional limp mode, fault often not reproducible

P0195.title: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit
P0195.description: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0195 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. With analogue sensors most manufacturers use P0197/P0198 instead. The documented use is Ford's 2023 diesels with a digital SENT oil temperature sensor: P0195 is set when the sensor reports a status or data fault for 5 s, while a complete loss of communication is U0667. The module then uses a substitute value (Saab: 100 °C), and functions relying on oil temperature are restricted.

causes.label: Connector or harness damaged, corroded or oil-soaked
Sensor faulty internally (electronics fault on SENT sensors)
5 V reference or ground problem in the sensor circuit
Control module or software

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature display missing or fixed
Restricted cam timing, slightly reduced power

P0196.title: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance
P0196.description: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0196 means the signal is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or rising wrongly. GM's LT4 runs three tests: after a cold soak oil, coolant and intake air must agree within 16 °C; during warm-up the oil must reach 90 °C after enough air mass; and continuously it is compared with a model (fault above 30 °C); two trips. Saab expects at least 50 °C once coolant has held 80 °C for 3 min. Caution: on Ford's 2023 diesels P0196 actually checks the coolant sensor against oil temperature (35 °C after 6 h), and Nissan traced it on the Rogue to a faulty coolant control valve.

causes.label: Oil temperature sensor drifting or stuck (offset)
Comparison sensor (coolant, intake air) or its wiring wrong
Thermal management or coolant control valve, or thermostat faulty (oil genuinely too hot or cold)
Contact resistance in the connector
Control module software

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drives)
Possibly a cam timing code alongside

P0197.title: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0197.description: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. A substitute value is used.

causes.label: Signal wire chafed against ground or the engine block
Sensor shorted internally
Oil or water in the connector (leakage current)
Control module input faulty

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature display at maximum or oil temperature warning
Fan running constantly or power reduction possible

P0198.title: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0198.description: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0198 means the signal sits near the 5 V reference, so the module sees extremely cold oil (below −40 °C) – typically an unplugged connector, a broken wire, an open sensor element or a short to voltage. The module uses a substitute value and Ford disables variable cam timing.

causes.label: Connector unplugged or pins corroded, signal or ground wire broken
Sensor element open
Signal wire shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Control module pull-up or input faulty

symptoms: Check engine light on (depending on manufacturer)
Oil temperature display stays at minimum or blank
Restricted cam timing, possibly slightly less power
Oil life monitor calculates with a substitute value

P0199.title: Engine Oil Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0199.description: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. causes.label: Loose contact or corroded pins at the sensor connector
Harness chafing intermittently (engine movement)
Sensor with internal hairline crack
Control module ground connection

symptoms: Check engine light or only a stored code

P019A.title: O2 Sensor Delayed Response - Rich to Lean Bank 1 Sensor 3
P019A.description: Sensor 3 on bank 1 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick; it exists on Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (on both banks) and on Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late after a mixture change – unlike 'slow response' (P0145/P0165), where the transition itself is too flat. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, tested during forced fuel cut-off. For sensor 2, GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before a calibrated air mass has passed; behind two converters their oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0142ff/P0162ff for sensor 3 – so the description rests on CARB's response requirement and the sensor 2 logic. There is no limp mode; the converter monitor cannot complete.

causes.label: Sensor 3 aged, sooted or oil-poisoned
Exhaust leak ahead of sensor 3
Converter with strongly differing oxygen storage (aftermarket or new)
Sensor 3 heater weak
Control module software

P019E.title: Alternative Fuel Tank A Pressure Sensor Circuit
P019E.description: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The tank pressure sensor A sits at or in the regulator; together with the tank temperature it gives the gas level, and it decides whether gas operation is possible. P019E is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. Ford's earlier bi-fuel CNG system showed the gauge as empty on a tank pressure sensor fault. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.

causes.label: Connector or harness at the tank pressure sensor (at the regulator) corroded, loose or chafed
Tank pressure sensor faulty
5 V reference or ground disturbed
Engine or alternative fuel control module faulty

symptoms: Gas level gauge wrong, jumping or showing empty
Gas operation blocked or automatic switch to petrol
Dedicated gas engines: limp mode or starting problems possible

P01CB.title: Cylinder 1 Injection Timing Performance - Over Retarded

From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.

causes.label: Injector worn, coked or sticking (opens late, delivers too little)
False setting from software or vehicle vibration (e.g. off-road tyres)
Wrong injector correction code stored after an injector replacement
Boost leak or loose injector clamp
Contaminated fuel

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P01E8.title: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open
P01E8.description: Engine coolant heater A is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports an open control circuit – the module detects missing continuity, typically with the driver switched off. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

causes.label: Control wire or connector to the heater or relay open
Heater element burnt out or relay coil open
Fuse in the load circuit blown
Control module output stage faulty

symptoms: Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter
