Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Control module output stage

symptoms: Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter

P01EE.title: Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit High
P01EE.description: Engine coolant heater B is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports a control circuit voltage that is too high – typically a short to battery voltage or overcurrent. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

causes.label: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Relay coil or heater with too low resistance (overcurrent)
Harness damage touching a positive wire
Control module

symptoms: Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter

P01EF.title: Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Performance
P01EF.description: Engine coolant heater B is an electric coolant heater switched by the engine module, directly or via a relay or power stage, to shorten warm-up – less cold-start emissions and faster cabin heat; A and B denote two separately switched heaters or stages. It is not the same as a mains-powered block heater (which the vehicle does not control) or the electrically heated thermostat (P0597–P0599). CARB requires output components to be checked for correct response or at least for circuit faults. This code reports that the heater circuit is electrically intact but the heater does not work as commanded – for example a sticking relay or a weak element. No manufacturer using these codes was found in the GM, Ford or NHTSA documents checked; the typical driver diagnosis (open circuit detected with the driver switched off, as GM does for other outputs) is an analogy, and thresholds are unknown.

causes.label: Relay sticking or not switching (burnt contacts)
Heater element aged or scaled, output too low
Voltage drop in the load circuit or switched off by power management
Low coolant or air at the heater

symptoms: Longer warm-up, cabin heat slower in winter

P01F0.title: Coolant Temperature Relapsed Below Diagnostic Monitoring Temperature
P01F0.description: Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check. GM sets it when coolant falls below 64 °C with a conventional thermostat or 70.5 °C with an electrically heated one (2019 Corvette: 65/78.5 °C) after having been above it, with at least 0.8 km driven, ambient above −7 °C, enough heat input and no long overrun downhill; two trips. GM also uses it on the 6.6 litre Duramax diesel as a 'stuck open thermostat' check. Ford does not use the code in the documents checked. Usual cause is a thermostat stuck open.

causes.label: Thermostat stuck open or not sealing
Heated map thermostat, thermal management valve or switchable water pump faulty
Radiator fan running constantly (relay stuck)
Coolant sensor drifting cold
Low coolant or air in the system

symptoms: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P01F1.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F1.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F1 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0136/P0142 for sensors 2 and 3. Typical causes are an aged sensor, open or high-resistance wiring and a failed heater.

causes.label: Sensor 4 aged or poisoned
Wiring or connector open, high-resistance or corroded
Sensor heater failed
Control module

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F2.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Low Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F2.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F2 means the signal stays near 0 V – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, a faulty sensor or an exhaust leak ahead of it; GM checks its other downstream sensors for a signal below about 40–60 mV.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor faulty
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F3.title: O2 Sensor Circuit High Voltage Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F3.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F3 means the signal is above about 1.05–1.1 V, which a switching sensor cannot produce – typically the heater supply or another voltage on the signal wire, or a heater-to-signal short inside the sensor.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Sensor faulty internally
Sensor ground open (bias logic)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F4.title: O2 Sensor Circuit Slow Response Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F4.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F4 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes; CARB requires at least a rich-to-lean response test of downstream sensors during fuel cut-off. Behind several converters the oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide.

causes.label: Sensor aged or contaminated
Exhaust leak ahead of the sensor
Sensor heater weak

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F5.title: O2 Sensor Circuit No Activity Detected Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F5.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F5 means that with a warm engine and heated sensor the signal does not switch between rich and lean but stays in the middle or at the bias voltage the module applies. For sensor 2, GM detects this when the signal stays above 1.7 V of a 1.9 V bias, a two-trip fault. Usual causes are an open signal or ground wire or a dead sensor.

causes.label: Signal or ground wire open, connector corroded
Sensor aged or poisoned, produces no voltage
Sensor heater faulty, sensor does not reach operating temperature
Exhaust leak upstream of the sensor

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F6.title: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F6.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F6 means the sensor stays lean: the module deliberately enriches the mixture, and if the sensor does not reach the expected rich voltage before a set amount of air has passed, it counts as stuck lean. GM runs this test on sensor 2 once per trip as a two-trip fault. Usual causes are an aged sensor, an exhaust leak ahead of it or a signal wire shorted to ground.

causes.label: Sensor aged, characteristic shifted lean
Exhaust leak or false air upstream of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to ground or contact resistance
Misfires or mixture fault (excess oxygen)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F7.title: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich Bank 1 Sensor 4
P01F7.description: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, downstream of a further converter. No manufacturer or vehicle using sensor 4 codes could be identified (GM and Ford documents stop at sensor 3); the description follows CARB's requirements for downstream sensors and GM's checks on sensor 2. P01F7 means the sensor stays rich: when the module leans the mixture or cuts fuel on overrun, the signal does not drop into the lean range. CARB names exactly this rich-to-lean transition during fuel cut-off as the minimum check for downstream sensors; GM tests sensor 2 this way as a two-trip fault. Usual causes are a sooted or oil-fouled sensor or a signal wire shorted to the heater supply.

causes.label: Sensor sooted, oil-fouled or aged
Signal wire shorted to voltage (e.g. heater supply)
Mixture genuinely rich (leaking injector, coolant or oil burning)

symptoms: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Catalyst monitor readiness possibly not set

P01F8.title: Engine Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F8.description: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater A are P01E8–P01EB.

causes.label: Short or partial short in heater element A
Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector
Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated
Heater running without coolant (low level, air pocket)

symptoms: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent)
Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather

P01F9.title: Engine Coolant Heater B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P01F9.description: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater B – a second heater or heating stage – through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater B are P01EC–P01EF.

causes.label: Short or partial short in heater element B
Wiring or connector chafed to ground, moisture in connector
Driver stage in the module or relay faulty or overheated

symptoms: Check engine light or warning message (manufacturer-dependent)
Slow warm-up, little heat in cold weather

P01FA.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit
P01FA.description: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FA is the general electrical fault that the module does not classify as low or high. Without a plausible actual pressure, boost control usually limits boost.

causes.label: Connector or pins at sensor B loose or corroded
Harness damaged (5 V reference, signal, ground)
Sensor faulty
Engine module or 5 V supply disturbed

P01FB.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Range/Performance
P01FB.description: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FB is the plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but does not fit. After a long stop all pressures should equal barometric pressure; while running the value is compared with a pressure modelled from airflow, speed and throttle – GM flags its boost sensor at deviations of roughly 25–30 kPa.

causes.label: Sensor drifting or stuck
Leaking charge air hose or blocked pressure port
Contact resistance at the connector
Fault in other model inputs (MAF, MAP)

P01FC.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low
P01FC.description: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FC means the signal voltage stays below its lower limit – usually a signal wire shorted to ground or a missing 5 V reference. For comparison, GM sets its boost sensor low code below 14.4 % of 5 V, Ford below 0.19 V for 5 s.

causes.label: Signal wire shorted to ground
5 V reference open or shorted
Sensor faulty internally

P01FD.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Circuit High
P01FD.description: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FD means the signal voltage stays above its upper limit – typically an open signal or sensor ground (the input is pulled up) or a short to voltage. For comparison, GM sets its boost sensor high code above 86 % of 5 V, Ford above 4.88 V.

causes.label: Sensor ground or signal wire open
Signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Sensor faulty

P01FE.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic
P01FE.description: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FE counts brief spikes or dropouts that are too short for the low or high code. Ford's equivalent boost sensor check sets after 10 such events in one drive cycle. The usual cause is a loose or corroded contact or a wire broken by vibration and heat.

causes.label: Loose contact or corroded connector
Wire breaking from vibration or heat
Sensor erratic internally

P01FF.title: Turbocharger Outlet Pressure Sensor A/B Correlation
P01FF.description: Turbocharger outlet pressure sensor B is a second pressure sensor at a compressor outlet – for example one per turbo on twin-turbo engines or a second measuring point; sensor A has the codes P00F8–P00FC. It is a separate family from the boost pressure sensor: GM and Ford report the pressure ahead of the throttle under the boost sensor codes P0236–P0238. No manufacturer using the sensor B codes was found; FCA documents sensor A and a second outlet sensor. P01FF compares sensors A and B: with the engine off both should read barometric pressure, and in comparable operation they must agree within a tolerance. If they disagree without either being electrically faulty, this code sets; which one is wrong is found by comparing with barometric and manifold pressure. On twin-turbo engines a genuinely weaker turbo on one bank can also cause it.

causes.label: One sensor drifting
Leak or hose damage between the measuring points or on one bank
Contact resistance at one sensor's connector or ground
Uneven turbo output (twin-turbo, wastegate or vanes on one side)
